title: Referrals and repeat work from existing clients for Personal and fitness training
audience: Personal trainers and fitness coaches who want repeat bookings, programme renewals and referrals from clients they have already trained.
learningOutcomes: Plan a review or referral request that is made after the client has agreed the programme is complete, and that the client can decline easily.
Write a next-block offer with a date, a scope and a price approach, and schedule the check-in that follows it.
Write referral reward terms, including the condition for payment, before any referral is made.

instruction.heading: Ask at the point the client is most satisfied
instruction.body: The best time to ask for a review or referral is after the client has agreed that a programme review is complete and is satisfied with what was delivered. In practice that is often the final review, or the day the last invoice is paid. Ask in one sentence, name the next step you would like, such as a review or the name of one person who might want sessions, and make it easy to decline. Record what you asked and what the client said. Timing matters. In one Baylor Keller Center experiment, 1.32 per cent of customers left reviews with no reminder, against 2.16 per cent with a late reminder (Baylor Keller Center, 1 June 2024). That is a single experiment, not a fitness study. The AMA says experience goods need more evaluation time than search goods (AMA, 10 January 2023), so a training programme, which the client experiences over weeks, is a reason to wait for the client's own review of the results. Do not write reviews for clients or invent them, and do not filter out unhappy clients. Asking only satisfied clients is 'review gating', which Podium, a review software vendor, says Google treats as a violation (Podium, 2 May 2022). Google bans discounts or goods in exchange for reviews, including for changing or removing negative reviews (Google Help, no date shown). The ACCC says incentives must be disclosed and must not depend on what the review says (ACCC, 15 July 2026).

instruction.heading: Offer the next block before the client leaves
instruction.body: Repeat work is a dependable source of growth for a small service business. At the final review, propose the next step with a date: a further 12-week block, a fortnightly session pattern, or a small group that continues the work. Put the scope, the interval, the price approach and any pause or renewal terms in writing, and confirm that the client agrees before you change their booking. State when any pack or block expires, so the client does not discover it later. If the written offer goes by email or text, check the electronic message rules first. ACMA's guidance says inferred consent is narrow and does not cover a message sent just after a purchase (ACMA, no date shown).

instruction.heading: Check in at an interval that suits the service
instruction.body: For a training programme, a check-in around ninety days is a suggested starting point to test, not a benchmark. The check asks whether the client's goal still holds, what has changed and whether they want the next block. Keep it short, record the reply and close the loop. Every commercial email or text needs an unsubscribe option, and ACMA says an unsubscribe must be honoured within five working days (ACMA, no date shown). A check-in that only asks about the result may not be commercial, but a message that promotes any service can be, even when it is framed as a reminder (Clayton Utz, 9 November 2023).

instruction.heading: Re-contact around renewal dates, not seasons
instruction.body: The research found no seasonal demand data for personal training, so do not plan around a season you have not measured. Plan a short message before each client's own renewal, pack expiry or planned break, using dates from your booking records. Offer slots you can deliver, on written terms, with a clear way to opt out. Do not pressure anyone, and do not contact a client who has asked not to hear from you. Record each opt-out as soon as you receive it and stop sending to that client. At the end of each cycle, note which timing produced a reply.

instruction.heading: Set referral rewards in writing before anyone refers
instruction.body: A referral reward works best when the client knows the terms before they refer someone. Decide what you will offer, such as a credit on the next block or a small thank-you, and write down the payment condition, which is normally that the referred person has completed a paid programme. Stating the referrer's reward in the invitation increased referring across a set of studies (Xu, Yu and Tu, Journal of Marketing Research, 2023). Get the referred person's consent before any referral message is sent, because the referrer's word alone may not be enough (Clayton Utz, 11 May 2017, an older source). Check any cash or credit reward, and its tax or contract effect, with an adviser. No business.gov.au or ACCC guidance on referral rewards was found, so those points are unconfirmed. Quantified referral data for personal training was not found, so this lesson gives no referral rate.

procedure: After the programme's final review is agreed, make one review or referral request, and record what was asked and the answer.
Write the next-block offer with a date, scope, interval, price approach and expiry terms, and confirm it with the client.
Schedule the check-in for the interval that suits the service, and send it using the electronic message rules.
Plan a re-contact message before each client's renewal or pack expiry, and exclude anyone who has opted out.
Write the referral reward terms and the payment condition before the first referral is made.
When a referral books, confirm the referred programme is paid before applying the reward, and record the outcome.
Review at the end of each season which requests, offers and timings produced repeat work.

workedExamples.situation: A personal trainer finishes a 12-week programme with a regular client. The client says she will recommend him to her brother, who lives nearby. She wants to offer her a credit on her next block if the brother signs up.
workedExamples.decisionPrompt: What should the trainer do before the brother books, and what should he avoid?
workedExamples.reasoning: He writes down the reward terms before any referral happens: the credit, the condition that the brother completes a paid block, and when the credit will be applied. He asks his client to pass on the brother's details, and he contacts the brother only if the brother agrees. He does not promise a reward he has not written down. If he is unsure of the tax or contract effect of the credit, he confirms it with an adviser. He does not take on any work that his qualifications and insurance do not cover.

equipmentAndPpe: Client record with the final review date and the review or referral request made
Next-block offer template with scope, interval, price approach and expiry terms
Calendar of renewal and pack-expiry dates taken from booking records
No PPE is needed for client follow-up; any session follows the venue's own safety rules

commonErrors.error: Asking for a review before the client has agreed the programme is complete.
commonErrors.prevention: Ask after the final review or payment, when the client has confirmed the result is right.

commonErrors.error: Offering a referral reward that was never written down, so the terms are disputed later.
commonErrors.prevention: Write the reward and its payment condition before any referral is made, and give the referrer a copy.

commonErrors.error: Publishing a client's name, photo, review or progress images without consent for that use.
commonErrors.prevention: Get consent for each thing you plan to publish, and keep the record.

commonErrors.error: Contacting a client who asked not to hear from you, or using a re-contact message to pressure them.
commonErrors.prevention: Keep an opt-out list, honour it at once, and keep re-contact messages factual and optional.

safetyAndRegulatory.point: Publishing a client's name, photo, review or progress images needs the client's consent for that use. Do not write reviews on a client's behalf or invent them. The OAIC says the Privacy Act 1988 (Cth) covers organisations with an annual turnover above $3 million and some other organisations, so check whether it applies to your business (OAIC, published 13 May 2026).

Review platforms and referral programmes can have their own rules on incentives. Google bans discounts or goods in exchange for reviews. The ACCC says incentives must be disclosed and must not depend on the review's content. Check each platform's rules before offering any reward.
Check-in and re-contact messages sent by email or text can be commercial electronic messages under the Spam Act 2003 (Cth). ACMA has been enforcing this area, so check each message before sending.

Renewal and auto-renewal: Victoria's guidance on health and fitness centre agreements (January 2011, may be superseded) treats auto-renewal as unfair unless the consumer can opt out at sign-up. A law-firm summary dated 3 July 2026 says new unfair trading practice rules take effect on 1 July 2027. That date is unverified, so check the legislation before you rely on it.

A referral does not extend your qualifications or insurance. Accept only the work your qualifications and insurance cover. Industry registration is optional under Better Health's guidance, but check your insurer's terms and your state's rules. This lesson does not grant any licence.

qualityStandard: Every review or referral request is made after the programme is agreed or paid, and it includes an easy way to decline.
Every next-block offer is written, has a date and expiry terms, and is confirmed by the client before the booking changes.
Every referral reward has written terms and a payment condition, and is paid only when that condition is met.
documentationEvidence: Review or referral request log with the date sent and the answer.
Next-block offers with the date, scope, interval, expiry and client confirmation.
Referral reward terms with the referral record and payment outcome.
summary: Ask for reviews and referrals after the client has agreed the programme is complete, and make it easy to say no.
Offer the next block in writing, with a date and expiry terms, before the client leaves.
Set referral rewards and their payment conditions in writing before anyone refers.

knowledgeChecks.question: When is the best time to ask a client for a review or referral?
options: Before the programme starts, so the client feels committed
After the client has confirmed the result is right
Only when the client has sent you a complaint

knowledgeChecks.question: A client wants to publish a review with their name and a photo of their training session. What do you need?
options: Their consent for the name and photo you plan to publish
Nothing, because the review is positive
Your own judgement that the photo looks professional

knowledgeChecks.question: What should a referral reward look like?
options: Paid to anyone who mentions your name
Decided after the referred person books, based on how keen the referrer seems
Decided and written in advance, with the condition for payment stated

knowledgeChecks.question: When does the lesson say to propose the next step for the client?
options: At the end of each job, with a date

AMA, 'Asking for customer reviews at the right time', https://www.ama.org/2023/01/10/asking-for-customer-reviews-at-the-right-time-sooner-is-not-always-better/, 10 January 2023. Supports: experience goods need more evaluation time.
Google Help, 'Business Profile review links', https://support.google.com/business/answer/3474122?hl=en-GB, no date shown. Supports: review links and the ban on rewards for reviews.

Xu, Yu and Tu, Journal of Marketing Research 60(2), 2023, https://research.polyu.edu.hk/en/publications/i-will-get-a-reward-too-when-disclosing-the-referrer-reward-incre/. Supports: stating the reward in the invitation. No figures used.

Clayton Utz, 'Referrer beware', https://www.claytonutz.com/insights/2017/may/referrer-beware-proceed-with-caution-when-contemplating-refer-a-friend-promotions, 11 May 2017. Older source; supports the referred person's consent.

Clayton Utz, 'The ACMA cranks up enforcement', https://www.claytonutz.com/insights/2023/november/the-acma-cranks-up-enforcement-do-your-factual-customer-emails-pass-the-spam-act-test, 9 November 2023. Supports: promotional service reminders can be commercial.

ACMA, 'Avoid sending spam', https://www.acma.gov.au/avoid-sending-spam, no date shown; read 2026-11-04 per research. Supports: unsubscribe honoured within five working days; inferred consent is narrow.

OAIC, 'Australian Privacy Principles guidelines', https://www.oaic.gov.au/privacy/australian-privacy-principles/australian-privacy-principles-guidelines/, published 13 May 2026. Supports: which organisations the Privacy Act covers.

Older; check currency.

officialReferences.title: Avoid sending spam
officialReferences.covers: Says commercial messages cannot be sent without the recipient's permission or consent; messages must accurately identify the sender and include correct contact details; every commercial message must contain an unsubscribe option under the Spam Act 2003. Does not mention one-to-one messages. Publisher: ACMA.

officialReferences.title: Online reviews for product and services (ACCC)
officialReferences.covers: Says incentives for reviews must be disclosed and must not depend on what the review says. Publisher: ACCC.

officialReferences.title: Australian Privacy Principles guidelines (OAIC)
officialReferences.covers: States that the Act covers organisations with an annual turnover above $3 million and some other organisations, without listing them. The full consent detail was not read; small business coverage is unconfirmed. Publisher: OAIC.
